dream_response:
The museum occupies the space between a lightning flash and the counting of the seconds afterward. From the street it looks like a narrow house with a green door. From inside, the street looks like something recalled under hypnosis.

It opens at the first thunderclap. Admission is one wet glove. Visitors who arrive barehanded may borrow a glove from the attendant, who will hold it briefly under the leaking ceiling before accepting it.

There are five exhibits.

### I. The Orchard Stone

A gray stone rests on a cushion worn flat at the center. It is warm enough that visitors sometimes set their chilled fingers against the glass.

Once each hour it gives off the smell of pears. The attendant opens a small vent in the case to let the scent out, then shuts it before the room becomes unbearable.

The brass placard reads:

> **STONE FROM THE LAST ORCHARD**  
> Date unknown  
>   
> Recovered after the trees, soil, and hill had been removed.  
>   
> Please do not describe the surrounding countryside within hearing of the specimen.

There is a shallow hollow on its underside. In old catalog photographs, the hollow is on top.

### II. A Length of Thursday

Eleven inches of pale ribbon hang in a case that is considerably deeper than the room containing it. The ribbon occasionally turns, showing a dark reverse.

Most visitors recognize the dark side as a day they spent indoors.

The brass placard reads:

> **THURSDAY, APPROXIMATELY 3:10–3:14 P.M.**  
> Silk, elapsed time  
> Gift of an anonymous schoolteacher  
>   
> This portion was removed without significantly shortening the week.  
> Do not pull loose threads.

A pin lies beneath it. The attendant insists the pin belongs to the case, although it appears in no inventory and is always a little farther to the left.

### III. The Harbor in a Tooth

The tooth stands root-down in a jeweler’s clamp. Through the magnifying lens above it, visitors can see a harbor inside the crown: a breakwater, six fishing boats, and a white customs house with washing drying from an upper window.

The tide comes in while you watch.

The brass placard reads:

> **LOWER MOLAR, PROVENANCE DISPUTED**  
> Enamel, dentin, municipal buildings  
>   
> No attempt has been made to contact the inhabitants.  
> The museum requests that visitors extend the same courtesy.

Beside the lens is a chair for anyone who recognizes the harbor. Its upholstery has been replaced twice this year.

### IV. The Instrument for Remembering Rain

It resembles a barometer built by someone who had seen a violin but misunderstood its purpose. Gut strings cross a pear-shaped brass body. Beneath the glass dial, a slender needle rests between **BEFORE** and **AGAIN**.

There is no keyhole, though a key hangs beside it.

The brass placard reads:

> **INSTRUMENT FOR REMEMBERING RAIN**  
> Maker unrecorded  
>   
> Acquired in working condition.  
> The precise nature of its work remains under review.  
>   
> Please refrain from humming.

Water collects in the display case. Staff empty it into a bucket kept beneath the stand. By closing time, the bucket contains a handful of dry leaves.

### V. Portrait of the Donor as an Empty Chair

The painting is small and badly lit. It shows a cane-backed chair in a room with yellow walls. A coat has been folded over one arm. Behind the chair, a window looks out on a garden at dusk.

The varnish is cracked everywhere except the coat.

The brass placard reads:

> **PORTRAIT OF THE DONOR AS AN EMPTY CHAIR**  
> Oil on linen  
> Artist and sitter unknown  
>   
> The terms of the donation require that the chair remain unoccupied.  
> No such restriction applies to the room.

If you stand close enough, you can hear someone in the painted garden working a spade into the ground. They stop whenever thunder makes the gallery windows shake, and resume a few moments later.

---

When the storm passes, the attendant collects the visitors from the galleries. Anyone reluctant to leave is permitted to take a postcard. The postcards show the green door in fine weather, standing alone in a vacant lot.

Pinned beneath the attendant’s desk is a note in the night custodian’s handwriting:

> Please leave the bucket where it is.
>
> I know about the leaves.
>
> Also, whoever keeps putting a second chair in the portrait: I have to go in there to take it out, and the garden path is getting longer.

dream_response:
The universe is roughly the size of a pear, although nobody has walked around it to check.

Its only law is this:

**Every closed loop contains a sea.**

Not a picture of a sea. Not some dampness. A sea, with depth and weather and things moving far below the reach of a spoon.

The first inhabitants discovered this while making a handle for a saucepan. The moment the blacksmith joined the ends, a wave came through his workshop and carried away his apprentice’s lunch.

Since then, saucepan handles have had gaps.

So have bracelets, fences, and the letter O, which is written with a little break at the top. Literacy was extremely dangerous before this convention. An early dictionary still lies at the bottom of the municipal square. On quiet evenings you can hear the whales in *balloon*.

Most people live in houses shaped like three sides of a rectangle. Privacy is achieved by staggering the walls. There are no doors, only corners to turn.

This is inconvenient in winter.

It is also inconvenient when you drop a wedding ring.

Mera dropped hers on a Tuesday. It rolled beneath the kitchen dresser, where it lay flat and began producing surf. By lunchtime the lowest drawer was full of kelp.

Her husband brought a broom.

“Don’t push it farther back,” Mera said.

“I’m not.”

“You are. I can hear the gulls getting smaller.”

They eventually retrieved it with a hooked wire, losing two potatoes and most of the afternoon. Mera put it back on her finger. A very distant storm moved across her knuckle.

Wedding rings are considered worth the trouble. Belts are not.

***

The seas are not all alike.

A loop of yellow thread generally contains warm, shallow water. Copper rings tend toward fog. A circle made by touching thumb to forefinger opens onto a sea so perfectly clear that people sometimes sit looking into their hands until somebody reminds them to eat.

Scientists have no explanation for these differences.

Their greatest unsolved problem, however, is the bell.

It hangs in the Institute of Joined Ends. Its mouth encloses a black sea without waves. When the bell is struck, ships can be heard answering.

No ship has ever been seen.

The answers arrive before the blow.

The institute employs a man whose entire job is to stand beside the bell and occasionally decide not to strike it. So far, the ships have never been wrong.

He dislikes his work, but the pension is excellent.

***

Fishing is mostly done with embroidery hoops.

A good fisher carries six or seven, each wrapped separately so their climates don’t spoil one another. You lower a line, wait, and pull up whatever has mistaken your bait for something plausible.

One afternoon a fisher named Pell caught a fish with a tiny iron hoop through its lip.

Inside the hoop was another sea.

Inside that sea, plainly visible because it happened to be a clear day, was a boat.

A person in the boat was fishing.

Pell leaned closer.

The person leaned closer too, although not toward Pell. Toward something beneath the boat.

Pell cut the line.

For several weeks he would eat only turnips.

At the tavern they told the old joke to cheer him up.

“Why did the sailor leave his soup unfinished?”

Pell waited.

“He wanted somewhere to stand.”

Everyone laughed except the visitor from the button islands, who had lost an uncle that way.

***

I should explain that I have been describing this universe from outside it.

It sits on my desk beside a chipped cup. Under a magnifying glass I can make out the Institute, the interrupted fences, Mera shaking salt from a dishcloth. When the light is right, I can even see the little man beside the bell, holding his hammer and trying to be unpredictable.

I had supposed the universe was self-contained.

Then yesterday I noticed that my cup’s handle is unbroken.

There was water inside it.

Not much. A dark, vertical patch where I would ordinarily put my finger.

I fetched the magnifying glass.

There was a ship.

On its deck stood a man beside a bell. He was looking up at me with an expression I initially mistook for awe.

He pointed behind me.

I turned.

Nothing.

When I looked back, he was laughing so hard he had to sit down.

The universe is a circular gutter, nine metres around. Outside its two low walls there is nothing—not darkness, but nowhere to put darkness. Overhead is enough sky for a tall person to raise an umbrella.

Most things behave ordinarily. There are three exceptions.

**First:** sound travels only clockwise, at one metre per second. It does not fade. A note can circle the gutter forever unless water catches it.

**Second:** when a note crosses the upstream edge of a puddle, the puddle absorbs it and throws one drop vertically upward from its downstream edge. The drop rises one millimetre for every vibration per second in the note. A low hum makes a modest hop. A shriek can wet the sky.

**Third:** the thrown drop remembers its note. If it lands in water, it releases that note clockwise from the puddle’s downstream edge. If it lands on anything dry, the note is lost.

These laws make conversation somewhat inconvenient.

You cannot call to someone immediately anticlockwise of you without everyone else hearing first. People saying private things stand with their mouths almost touching their listeners’ upstream ears. Beyond the listener they hold a little cup of water, with felt stretched over it to catch the departing drop.

This is called closing your mouth properly.

Rain is uncommon, but arguments can produce it.

At first the gutter had eleven puddles, separated by dry stretches of brass. Sounds passed from puddle to puddle, spending part of each journey as drops. Low notes hurried. High notes took longer, because they had farther to fall.

A spoon dropped in the third puddle made a complicated clatter. By its twentieth circuit, the clatter had come apart. Its lowest notes were several puddles ahead of its highest. Soon no one could recognize the spoon in it.

There was instead a procession.

Each puddle raised a small spray, rested, raised a taller spray, rested again. In some places two returning notes arrived together and lifted a pair of drops. Elsewhere the gutter stood quiet for almost a minute.

The inhabitants put stepping-stones between the puddles. They learned where not to leave laundry.

Then somebody moved a stone.

It was an unremarkable act. The stone had been digging into her heel.

In its new position, one corner projected over the edge of a puddle. The low-flying drops still returned to water, but a few higher ones struck the dry stone. Their notes disappeared.

Over the following days, more notes met the corner and were extinguished. What remained was a small company of pitches whose timing kept bringing them through while the stone was wet from other splashes.

The wetness mattered. A drop could surrender its note to even the shallowest film.

Eventually the company settled into a peculiar arrangement: three little notes wetted the corner, and a fourth, much higher note landed on it before it dried.

Then the four went round again.

Nobody had arranged this.

They called it the limper, because every ninth circuit it paused noticeably at the seventh puddle. It had no particular location. Sometimes most of it was airborne. Sometimes it was four sounds travelling across separate stretches of brass.

It could be killed with a towel.

It could also be divided. If someone caught a returning drop in a spoon and poured half into one puddle and half into another, both portions released the remembered pitch. Usually the resulting commotion soon lost notes against something dry. Once, however, a second procession survived.

That one did not limp.

By winter there were six, although winter here meant only that somebody had opened the cold cupboard.

—

I wake before the kettle and put my feet over the edge of the bed.

The brass is cool. Across the room, four drops rise from the washbasin: three barely clear the rim; the last hangs briefly beside the toothbrushes.

I wait for it to fall before taking the basin away.

There. That’s everyone past.

I pour a little clean water into the saucer on the floor, so they will have somewhere to go when they come round again.

## MUSEUM OF OBJECTS
### North Gallery

**1. THE EXTRA INTEGER**  
*Graphite on ruled paper*  
Accession 1908.14

An integer strictly between seven and eight. It is not a fraction, an approximation, or a numeral from another system. Division by it produces the expected results.

The sheet was removed from the accounts of a defunct laundry in Ghent. For thirty-one years, its proprietor charged this number of centimes for a collar. The business was profitable, and all surviving accounts balance.

**Provenance:** Estate of Marguerite Voss, bookkeeper. Donated by her nine children, of whom there were eight.

**Handling:** Count the corners of the sheet before and after moving it. If the totals differ, use the smaller number on the condition report.

---

**2. RELIEF WITHOUT LOSS**  
*Sealed glass ampoule; contents apparently clear*  
Accession 1962.03

The relief felt by a woman upon learning that her son had not been born.

The woman loved her son. The son existed, was unharmed, and was sitting beside her when the ampoule was filled. No fear, regret, resentment, or wish for a different life has been detected in the sample.

Visitors sometimes report recognizing the contents. Under examination, they invariably describe something else.

**Provenance:** Collected at St. Agnes Maternity Hospital during a routine calibration of the ward thermometer. Transferred from the hospital’s lost-property cupboard.

**Handling:** Keep upright. Do not warm in the hands. Staff exposed to a broken seal should be offered a chair, but not reassurance.

---

**3. TEASPOON**  
*Nickel silver*  
Accession 1987.221

A standard domestic teaspoon, showing wear consistent with approximately forty years of use.

Its bowl has an underside but no upper surface. It nevertheless holds four millilitres of liquid. The feature is easiest to observe while washing it, when the thumb fails to meet the forefinger by the thickness of a spoon.

It was used daily before acquisition. The former owner recalled nothing unusual about it, except that sugar took slightly longer to dissolve.

**Provenance:** Purchased with eleven other spoons at a house clearance in Norwich. The remaining spoons are in the staff kitchen.

**Handling:** Wash by hand. Dry without looking directly into the bowl. Return to the drawer face up, as far as this is possible.

---

**4. [LABEL WITHHELD]**  
*Materials not recorded*  
Accession 1934.00

The case and its contents form a single accession.

**Provenance:** Receipt retained in the director’s office.

**Handling:** Do not discuss.

*Please do not ask gallery attendants about this exhibit. They have read the same label you have.*

---

**5. MODEL OF A HOUSE, WITH ONE OPEN WINDOW**  
*Painted wood, glass, cotton curtains*  
Accession 2001.09

A scale model of a two-storey house, made with unusual attention to interior fittings. The front bedroom contains an empty wardrobe. A narrow bed stands beneath the open window.

At acquisition, the window was closed.

The model has remained fixed to its original base. However, the east-facing rooms are now three millimetres shallower than recorded in the accession photographs. A small quantity of plaster dust has appeared outside the museum’s east wall each spring.

The discrepancy is under review.

**Provenance:** Delivered by ordinary post. The parcel bore the museum’s address but was franked with a stamp depicting the house.

**Handling:** Do not close the window. Leave the gallery door ajar after dusk. Report any draught at floor level without attempting to locate its source.

---

Dr. Vale—

The little house hasn’t lost any more depth. I checked it against the marks you left.

Could you check the gallery instead? There are thirty-six floor tiles between the case and the east wall now. There were thirty-seven when I started here. I still have the old waxing sheet, with the rows numbered.

Also, please stop putting the spoon back in the exhibition drawer. The one you want is still in the kitchen. I know they look alike. Ours is the one that comes clean.

As for case four, nobody told us not to talk about it. We agreed.

The sound carries at night.

In the basin of Or, a hole is not obliged to remain in the material in which it was made.

This is the only respect in which the basin is unusual. Water runs downhill. Iron rusts. A dropped peach bruises on the side that strikes the ground.

But a hole drilled through a plank will, over several days, wander along the grain. The wood closes behind it and opens ahead. No sawdust is produced. The displaced substance travels around the hole’s circumference, slowly enough that a carpenter can see the swelling on the advancing side.

Across the grain, a hole travels more reluctantly. Through a knot, almost never.

A hole reaching the edge of a plank becomes a notch and ceases to wander. This is the usual method of disposal.

Two holes that meet become one hole of their combined area. They cannot separate again without intervention. Consequently, old colanders have three or four large openings and are used for quite different things than new colanders.

—

The first measurements were made with a brass plate and nine holes of equal diameter.

The investigator, Eda Ven, hung the plate vertically. Eight holes descended. The ninth climbed to a soldered patch and remained there.

From this she established that openings tend toward places where the material is easiest to displace. Gravity matters, but so do warmth, grain, fatigue, and the little strains left in metal by hammering. A hole does not fall like a stone. It travels more like a crease.

In the smoothest substances, motion is exceptionally slow. A glass washer may keep its opening centered for a hundred years. In lead, the same opening can reach the edge before lunch.

Ven’s surviving plate is kept flat in a cool room. Its present single hole is not considered a defect in the exhibit.

The label still says *Nine Openings of Equal Diameter*.

—

The basin’s plants are mostly broad-leaved.

An insect that chews through a leaf makes a mobile opening, and the veins guide it outward. Healthy leaves rid themselves of small holes in a few hours. After a hard season, the woodland has an intricate, ragged appearance, though the middle of each leaf remains whole.

One species of beetle exploits this. It bites a hole near the stem and lays an egg against the hole’s rim. As the opening migrates, the egg travels with it. At the leaf’s edge, the young beetle drops onto the undergrowth.

Its chief predator waits below particularly well-veined trees.

Flesh also carries openings, but living tissue is good at holding them. Around every mouth, nostril, and ear canal, cells perform a continuous, minute rebuilding. This costs food. Animals with many external openings must eat more than similarly sized animals with few.

During famine, the small mammals of Or develop narrowed ears.

Fish have their difficulties elsewhere.

—

The language distinguishes between making a hole and giving a hole somewhere to go.

You *bore* a beam. You *offer* it a neighboring beam.

An opening may pass between pieces of wood if their edges are joined closely enough. A good joiner can offer a doorway from one panel to another without interrupting its passage. A bad joiner leaves it stranded across the seam, with a bulge where the displaced wood cannot get through.

There is also a verb meaning *to discover that an opening has arrived*.

It is used for leaks, unexpected windows, and certain medical complaints. Its past tense is irregular.

People do not ask, “Where is the keyhole?”

They ask, “Where has the lock kept it?”

—

Buildings in Or have thick stone jambs, glazed drains, and windows surrounded by bands of harder material.

The bands are not decoration, although fashions have accumulated around them. A cheap window has an iron collar. An expensive one has a ring of polished green stone. The difference is partly practical: iron expands on hot afternoons, giving the opening room to shift and crack the glass.

Doorways are usually built down to the floor, making them interruptions in an edge rather than enclosed holes. There is nothing mobile about them.

This was not always understood.

The oldest houses have very high thresholds.

Their occupants used to wake and find that they needed a ladder to leave.

In the new district, walls have designated soft strips along which unwanted openings can travel toward a courtyard. Maintenance workers warm these strips with covered lamps. A nail hole may take a week to reach the collection edge. A rat hole goes faster.

The workers are paid by area, not by number.

—

At number twelve, Low Terrace, a pantry ventilation hole passed through the shared wall into the pantry of number fourteen.

It was a modest opening, about the size of a plum.

Mrs. Iven, at number twelve, wanted it back.

Mr. Sarr, at number fourteen, said it was not hers. It had come out of the wall, and the wall was jointly owned.

“I paid to have it drilled,” said Mrs. Iven.

“You paid to have plaster removed,” said Mr. Sarr. “You still have the benefit of its removal. Your house is no heavier.”

Mrs. Iven pointed out that her onions were sweating.

Mr. Sarr said his were keeping beautifully.

The terrace steward examined the wall. There was a nail above the opening on Mr. Sarr’s side, driven in at an angle that pressed the plaster and discouraged further travel.

Mr. Sarr said it had always been there.

There was no dust on it.

The steward’s provisional ruling required Mr. Sarr to remove the nail but did not require him to cool his pantry, which was warmer than Mrs. Iven’s and therefore likely to retain the hole.

Mrs. Iven began keeping a small lamp against the wall.

Mr. Sarr moved his flour.

It has one unusual property.

**At any point, draw a vertical line upward to the luminous ceiling. Count how many times that line crosses nightglass. If the count is even, gravity pulls downward. If it is odd, gravity pulls upward.**

Nightglass itself always falls downward. Everything else obeys the rule.

High on the cavern’s pillars, nightglass grows outward in enormous mineral leaves.

Beneath a leaf, warm air rises toward its underside. Beyond its edge, air settles toward the floor. The resulting circulation makes each leaf the center of a standing weather system.

Clouds gather underneath them.

When their droplets become heavy enough, rain falls upward and strikes the glass. Water collects against the underside, held there by gravity, until the wind pushes it over an edge. There it falls toward the ground.

Thus the country’s waterfalls have no rivers above them. They pour from the edges of transparent leaves, fed by lakes you can stand beneath and look into.

Where two leaves overlap, gravity points downward again. Their overlapping portions have dry undersides, and rain descends through the middle of an otherwise upward-falling storm.

Weather maps resemble lace.

For shelter, one plus one is zero.

## The mathematics of almost: *Paragenics*

Paragenics studies events that failed to occur but remain close enough to reality to be irritating.

Its fundamental object is a **near-event**
\[
N=(H,a,S,w),
\]
where \(H\) is a finite tree of possible histories, \(a\) is the actual state, \(S\) is the set of states in which the event has happened, and \(w\) assigns a positive revision cost to each edge.

A cost might measure seconds, money, effort, or embarrassment. These units must not be mixed without a conversion rule, which explains why the field’s economics department is so unpopular.

### Three axioms

**I. History branches.**  
\(H\) is a rooted tree, with edges directed away from the root. Moving forward follows a possible history. Moving backward is a counterfactual operation: it means revising what has already happened, not physically traveling through time.

Because \(H\) is a tree, every state has exactly one past.

**II. Occurrence persists.**  
The success set \(S\) is nonempty and contains every descendant of each of its members. The actual state \(a\) is not in \(S\).

An event, once it has happened, remains something that has happened. Sending a second letter saying “Please disregard my previous letter” does not unsend the first. This is an axiom rather than a courtesy.

**III. Revision adds.**  
Every edge has strictly positive cost. The cost of revising one state into another is the sum of the edge costs along their unique connecting path, ignoring direction.

The **almost-distance** is
\[
\delta(N)=\min_{s\in S}d(a,s).
\]

Thus, “almost” is not a separate kind of reality. It is a distance from reality to a specified success.

A second quantity records what distance alone conceals:
\[
\rho(N)=\min_{s\in S}d\bigl(a,\operatorname{lca}(a,s)\bigr),
\]
where \(\operatorname{lca}\) is the last common ancestor.

This is the **regret depth**: how much past must be reopened before success becomes possible.

- If \(\rho=0\), success is still available by going forward.
- If \(\rho>0\), some past choice or circumstance must change.

An unsent letter may have zero regret depth. A particular train, once missed, does not.

Both may nevertheless have the same almost-distance.

---

### One surprisingly useful theorem

**The Two-Pass Rescue Theorem.**  
*For a history tree with \(n\) states, the almost-distance from every state to success can be computed in \(O(n)\) time.*

This is useful because the obvious procedure—compare every state with every successful state—can take quadratic time.

First work upward from the leaves. Let \(b(v)\) be the cheapest success reachable by moving only forward from \(v\):
\[
b(v)=
\begin{cases}
0,&v\in S,\\
\min\limits_{c\text{ child of }v}\bigl(w(v,c)+b(c)\bigr),&v\notin S.
\end{cases}
\]
An empty minimum is infinity.

Then work downward from the root:
\[
D(r)=b(r),
\qquad
D(c)=\min\bigl(b(c),\,w(v,c)+D(v)\bigr)
\]
for each child \(c\) of \(v\).

The result is \(D(v)=d(v,S)\).

**Why it works:** Every shortest revision goes backward to one branching point and then forward toward success. It never needs to change direction twice. Positive costs ensure that wandering around feeling bad cannot improve the answer.

**Practical consequence:** A planner can identify the cheapest repair for every possible failure in two sweeps through its decision tree. The cheapest repair need not involve the latest mistake. Sometimes the optimal intervention is “leave five minutes earlier”; sometimes it is “do not accept the job in that city.”

The theorem does not distinguish between these emotionally.

---

### One unresolved conjecture

**The Conjecture of Recoverable Regret.**

Take an unweighted history tree with a single successful leaf. At every other vertex, record the pair
\[
(\delta,\rho).
\]

The conjecture says that, **among rooted trees in which no vertex has exactly one child and no two sibling subtrees are isomorphic**, the unordered multiset of these pairs uniquely determines the tree, including its successful leaf.

In plain language:

> If we know how close everyone came, and how far back everyone would have to go, can we reconstruct what happened?

The restrictions exclude simple ambiguities caused by repetitive branches and unnecessary intermediate states. Whether subtler ambiguities remain is unresolved in paragenics.

Professor Mara Venn calls it “the central reconstruction problem.”

Professor Ivo Rusk calls it “a census of disappointments pretending to be a biography.”

Neither has proved anything.

---

## The Venn–Rusk correspondence

The dispute began with two diagrams.

**A missed train:**
```text
             platform
             /      \
           1/        \1
           /          \
    boarded [S]     missed [a]
```

**An unsent letter:**
```text
       drafted [a]
            |
            |2
            |
         sent [S]
```

Both have almost-distance \(2\).

The train has regret depth \(1\). The letter has regret depth \(0\).

These facts were agreed upon. Everything else became expensive.

### From Venn, “On the Equivalence of Terminal Hesitations”

> A missed train and an unsent letter are the same scalar near-event: each is represented by its minimum revision cost. In the examples above, both represent \(2\).
>
> The difference between them belongs to the discarded history, not the scalar object under examination.

### Rusk’s referee report

> Professor Venn obtains her equivalence by discarding precisely the structure that distinguishes the objects.
>
> Under the natural definition of isomorphism—a root-preserving, direction-preserving, weight-preserving tree isomorphism carrying actuality to actuality and success to success—the two diagrams are plainly nonisomorphic.
>
> One can still send the letter. One cannot still board the departed train.
>
> I regret that this observation requires publication.

### Venn’s response

> I explicitly said *scalar* near-event.
>
> Professor Rusk’s objection is equivalent to rejecting the statement that two people have the same height because one of them is Professor Rusk.
>
> I agree that this is an important difference. It is not a difference in height.

### Rusk, in a subsequent paper

> The scalar quotient is mathematically legitimate and informationally impoverished. It identifies every example of almost-distance \(2\), including a locked door, a spoiled soufflé, and whatever Professor Venn currently means by an argument.
>
> My objection is not to taking a quotient. It is to advertising the quotient as a revelation.

“Do you deny that abstraction is foundational to mathematics?”

“No,” said Rusk. “I deny that removing the deadline from a missed train is an abstraction that leaves the interesting part intact.”

“You model every unsent letter as still sendable.”

“In the displayed example, it is.”

“And if the recipient has died?”

“Then it is a different tree.”

“And if the letter has been burned?”

“A different tree.”

“And if the writer has spent eleven years insisting that silence is a form of intellectual integrity?”

The chair asked whether this was still a question about finite trees.

“It is,” said Venn. “The tree is remarkably finite.”

### Email from Rusk to Venn, 11:48 p.m.

**Subject: Your example**

> The letter was not unsent.
>
> It was sent to your old departmental address and returned.
>
> You changed institutions without telling me.

### Reply from Venn, 12:03 a.m.

> Then your success set was “place envelope in postal system,” whereas mine was “receive an answer.”
>
> A remarkably convenient boundary condition.

### Rusk, 12:11 a.m.

> You missed the train deliberately.

### Venn, 12:14 a.m.

> You said you would ask me to stay.

### Rusk, 12:19 a.m.

> That is not in the published tree.

### Venn, 12:20 a.m.

> No, Ivo.
>
> It is in the revision.

Mera maintained the sharing.

“My back door,” he said. “Not lost. Longer.”

“Enough that I brought my lunch.”

She measured it.

Six feet ten inches. Its usual inch, and all her missing reserve.

“It would lift the floor.”

An event is an open subset \(E\) of a space \(X\). To happen is to belong to \(E\).

These are the places where the event can be approached arbitrarily closely, but has not happened.

Two events are contrary if

No single place permits both to happen.

## Preterition Theory

*An invented branch of mathematics, built on ultrametric geometry.*

Preterition theory studies things that did not happen, ordered by how much of the world would have to change for them to have happened.

Its central distinction is between **lateness** and **distance**. A train missed by ten seconds is temporally close. Whether catching it belongs to a nearby life is a separate question.

### Three axioms

**I. There is an actual history.**

A system consists of a nonempty set \(H\) of possible histories, one distinguished history \(r\)—the history that happened—and a finite revision distance \(d(x,y)\).

Revision distance is symmetric and nonnegative, and
\[
d(x,y)=0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x=y.
\]

The distance measures the scale of the alteration required to turn one history into another. It does not measure probability, desirability, or elapsed time.

**II. Revisions are nested.**

For any histories \(x,y,z\),
\[
d(x,z)\leq \max\{d(x,y),d(y,z)\}.
\]

Thus two small revisions cannot, merely by being combined, cross a larger historical divide. Possible histories have the geometry of a branching tree: their separation is the scale of the fork at which they part.

**III. Possibility has no missing limits.**

The space \(H\) is compact under \(d\): every sequence of histories has a subsequence converging to a history in \(H\).

An *event* is a nonempty closed subset \(E\subseteq H\). Its **miss-distance** is
\[
m_r(E)=\min_{e\in E}d(r,e).
\]

The minimum exists by compactness. If \(r\notin E\), it is strictly positive.

An event *almost happened at scale \(\varepsilon\)* when
\[
0<m_r(E)\leq\varepsilon.
\]

“Almost,” in this field, always requires a scale.

### One beautiful theorem: The Unmoved Horizon

**If one missed event is nearer than another, entering the nearer event by its smallest revision does not bring the farther event any closer.**

Precisely, suppose
\[
m_r(A)<m_r(B),
\]
and choose a nearest history \(a\in A\). Then
\[
m_a(B)=m_r(B).
\]

**Proof.** For every \(b\in B\),
\[
d(r,a)<d(r,b).
\]
The nested-revision axiom gives
\[
d(a,b)\leq\max\{d(a,r),d(r,b)\}=d(r,b).
\]
In the other direction,
\[
d(r,b)\leq\max\{d(r,a),d(a,b)\}.
\]
Since \(d(r,a)<d(r,b)\), this forces \(d(a,b)\geq d(r,b)\).

Hence \(d(a,b)=d(r,b)\) for every \(b\in B\). Taking minima proves the theorem. \(\square\)

> A small correction cannot reach across a larger fork.

It says nothing about which corrections are small. That is where most disputes begin.

k=\left\lfloor\frac N2\right\rfloor+1.

For every \(k\)-element subset containing the actual history \(r\), preserve its complete table of revision distances and mark which history is actual. Then erase all other identifying labels, leaving only the collection of these partial tables, with repetitions retained.

# The Museum of Almost

The museum occupies the space between two buildings whose original plans show a shared wall. Its collection is arranged by the reason each object failed to exist. The galleries are marked **SUPERSEDED**, **UNSELECTED**, **INCOMPATIBLE**, **INTERRUPTED**, and **UNRESOLVED**.

### 1. The Conservation of Nearness
*Superseded*

Under this law, objects that remained close together gradually became more difficult to separate.

Not through attraction. They exerted no force on one another. Instead, the intervening space acquired a resistance to being enlarged, proportional to the duration of the objects’ proximity. A cup could sit beside a saucer for a minute without consequence. After a century, moving it away would require the work of lifting a small house.

The law survived for approximately four seconds during an early revision of the universe. It was abandoned because it prevented anything from expanding unevenly. Stars could form, but their planets could never quite leave them enough room.

The exhibit contains two iron washers on a felt pad. They were cast together during those four seconds, although the iron itself is considerably younger.

Each morning, an attendant slides a piece of cigarette paper between them. The paper goes in easily. Pulling it out takes both hands.

### 2. The Unselected Color
*Unselected*

The color would have been visible to a coastal animal with four kinds of retinal cone.

Three of its cones were much like ours. The fourth responded to a narrow band between green and blue, while a separate neural circuit compared that response against the other three. This would have created an additional direction in color perception: not a new shade along a familiar spectrum, but a way for two apparently identical surfaces to differ.

The mutation arose in a population of burrowing mollusks eleven million years ago. Their larvae had the necessary eyes. Their adult bodies absorbed them before sexual maturity, and nothing in the larvae’s brief lives rewarded the distinction.

The museum cannot display the color. It displays two ceramic tiles that would have contrasted sharply in it.

To human visitors, both tiles are pale gray.

One has a fingerprint in the glaze. Under the proposed visual system, the fingerprint would be legible from the far end of the room.

### 3. The Deferred Present
*Incompatible*

This grammatical tense developed in a language that almost emerged among river settlements where messages routinely overtook their senders.

It described an action happening now whose status as a present event depended on something occurring later.

A speaker might say, in the deferred present, “I am meeting you at the landing.” This would mean neither an intention nor a prediction. The meeting was understood to be presently real but not yet settled. If the addressee eventually arrived, both parties would refer to the earlier waiting as part of the meeting. If not, the original sentence had not been false. It had lost its tense.

Children were expected to master the distinction before learning to count beyond twenty.

The exhibit is a page from an unwritten elementary reader. A woman sits at a table beside an empty chair. Below her is the sentence conventionally translated as:

**We are eating together, unless you never come.**

The verb has a small hook under its final character. In the margin, a teacher has drawn the hook three more times, each larger than the last.

*Interrupted*

For a brief period in the development of a continent, a shallow salt basin came close to becoming a sea governed by pressure rather than gravity.

A porous mineral layer connected the basin to a vast underground reservoir. Twice a day, heat passing through the surrounding rock would have expanded trapped gas, displacing water upward through millions of fine channels. The cycle would not have followed the moon. It would have followed the temperature of the previous afternoon, delayed and softened by stone.

A fault opened before the system reached equilibrium. The gas escaped over nine years. The basin dried into a deposit of ordinary salt.

Human memory reconstructs places from incomplete information. In most circumstances, discrepancies between two recollections remain discrepancies.

This exhibit concerns a possible exception.

If two people remembered the same nonexistent room in sufficient, independently maintained detail, the room might have acquired a limited spatial consistency. One cuff is still damp.

*Not for the collection catalogue*

The difficulty with the fifth exhibit is the cupboard.

### Recessional Geometry

Recessional geometry studies rooms whose dimensions are determined by what the sleeper has forgotten.

Its notation is simple. A room is written as a finite string:

\[
[a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n],
\]

where each \(a_i\) is something forgotten while entering: a name, a task, the reason for coming upstairs. The empty string, \([]\), denotes waking.

The same omission can occur more than once. Forgetting your mother’s voice is not the same operation the second time.

### Three axioms

**I. Every room has a finite address.**  
Two rooms are identical if and only if their lists of omissions are identical, in the same order.

**II. Returning removes the last omission.**  
Every nonempty room has exactly one return door:

\[
[a_1,\ldots,a_n]\longrightarrow[a_1,\ldots,a_{n-1}].
\]

You may find other doors, but they are entrances.

**III. Agreement determines distance.**  
For distinct rooms \(x\) and \(y\),

\[
d(x,y)=2^{-k},
\]

where \(k\) is the length of their longest common initial string. As usual, \(d(x,x)=0\).

Thus two rooms are close not because their walls touch, but because reaching them required almost the same losses.

These axioms hold only while dreaming. Awake, one cannot reliably distinguish forgetting something from forgetting that one has forgotten it. The addresses become unreadable.

### The theorem of the equal approaches

**Among any three distinct rooms, the two greatest distances are equal.**

To prove it, take the longest initial string shared by all three addresses. At the next position, either all three diverge, or two continue together and the third does not. In the first case, all three distances are equal. In the second, the third room is equally far from the other two, which are closer to each other.

There are no scalene triangles.

A consequence much admired by the first recessional geometers is this:

**If you move closer to one of two equally distant rooms, you do not move farther from the other.**

There is, for once, no price.

### The counterexample

For many years, students were also taught that any journey whose remaining steps became arbitrarily small must approach a room.

Consider:

\[
r_1=[a_1],\quad
r_2=[a_1,a_2],\quad
r_3=[a_1,a_2,a_3],\quad\ldots
\]

For \(m>n\),

\[
d(r_n,r_m)=2^{-n}.
\]

The journey is Cauchy: eventually, every remaining room lies as close to every other as you please.

But it approaches no room admitted by the first axiom. Any finite address eventually stops agreeing.

In the metric completion, its destination would be

\[
[a_1,a_2,a_3,\ldots].
\]

An infinite address.

No last omission.

No return door.

This does not refute the theorem. It refutes something the geometers had been less careful about saying.

The example appeared in the first edition of *An Introduction to Recessional Geometry*. In later editions, the page number remains, but the page does not.

Lovers developed customs of deliberate vagueness.

“You have wonderful eyes.”

“I couldn’t possibly say.”

# The Theory of Unarrivals
*From an imaginary monograph by Ada Venn and Elias Rook*

Ordinary probability studies what might happen. Unarrival theory studies something narrower:

**What can survive every finite attempt to rule it out, without ever occurring?**

Its primitive object is not a possibility but a succession of permissions.

## The three axioms

Let \(X\) be the set of things that actually happen—the *world*. At each depth \(n\), an observation \(p_n\) assigns each occurrence a finite record from a set \(O_n\).

The founders impose three axioms.

### I. Finite sight

Each \(O_n\) is finite. At depth zero there is only one record: *something happened*.

No finite observation can contain an infinite distinction.

### II. No retraction

Every record at depth \(n+1\) determines its record at depth \(n\). There are maps
\[
r_n:O_{n+1}\to O_n
\]
such that
\[
p_n=r_n\circ p_{n+1}.
\]

One may discover more, but one cannot discover that one previously observed something else.

### III. Local honesty

Every record in every \(O_n\) is realized by some member of \(X\). Moreover, any two different members of \(X\) eventually have different records.

Thus no finite possibility is fictitious, and no two occurrences remain indistinguishable forever.

Notice what is **not** required: that one occurrence realize an entire coherent infinite sequence of records.

That omission is the subject.

---

A **thread** is a sequence
\[
a=(a_0,a_1,a_2,\ldots),\qquad r_n(a_{n+1})=a_n.
\]

Every actual occurrence supplies a thread. But there may be others.

A thread not supplied by any member of \(X\) is called an **unarrival**.

Every finite part of an unarrival happened somewhere. The whole of it happened nowhere.

The set of all threads is denoted \(\widehat X\). Two threads are close when they agree for a long time: if their first disagreement occurs at depth \(k\), their distance is \(2^{-k}\).

Because each level has only finitely many records, \(\widehat X\) is compact. Because every finite record is realized, \(X\) is dense in it.

Venn called \(\widehat X\) *the completed world*.

Rook called it *the catalogue of our refusal to finish checking*.

## A specimen

Let \(X\) consist of all infinite binary sequences that eventually become permanently zero. Observing to depth \(n\) means reading the first \(n\) digits.

Then
\[
111111\ldots
\]
is an unarrival.

Any finite initial stretch of ones occurs in some member of \(X\). There is always an occurrence that agrees for longer. There is never one that agrees forever.

This is not an event of very small probability. No probability has been assigned.

It is an event whose every finite excuse is valid.

## The beautiful theorem

### The Unfinishable Distinction Theorem

**There is an unarrival if and only if the world can be divided into two nonempty outcomes such that:**

1. **Every actual occurrence reveals its outcome after finitely many observations.**
2. **No fixed number of observations suffices for all occurrences.**

In other words: *each case can be settled, but the question cannot be settled in advance.*

### Proof

Suppose first that an unarrival \(a\) exists.

Let \(C_n\) be the actual occurrences agreeing with \(a\) through depth \(n\). These sets are nonempty and nested, but
\[
\bigcap_n C_n=\varnothing.
\]

Discard repeated sets, leaving a strictly shrinking sequence
\[
D_0=X\supsetneq D_1\supsetneq D_2\supsetneq\cdots.
\]

Color the successive shells
\[
D_j\setminus D_{j+1}
\]
alternately blue and gold.

Every actual occurrence lies in a shell. A sufficiently detailed observation identifies that shell, so its color is eventually known.

But arbitrarily close to the missing thread there are shells of both colors. No observation depth decides every case.

Conversely, suppose such a division exists. At each depth there must be some record compatible with both colors; otherwise that depth would decide all cases.

These ambiguous records form a finitely branching tree with nodes at arbitrarily large depths. It therefore has an infinite path.

That path cannot represent an actual occurrence: by assumption, every actual occurrence eventually reveals its color.

It is an unarrival. \(\square\)

---

The theorem gives absence an unexpected signature.

One need not look for the missing occurrence directly. One may instead look for a distinction that is locally answerable but globally inexhaustible.

For any such blue–gold division, the set
\[
H=\overline{\text{Blue}}\cap\overline{\text{Gold}}
\]
inside \(\widehat X\) is called its **hesitation boundary**.

Its members are approached by both outcomes. None actually has either.

The founders agreed that this formula was the central result of their work. They disagreed about whether it described a wound or a seam.

## One unresolved conjecture

### The Equal Hesitation Conjecture

Consider the space of all infinite binary sequences, with the usual fair-coin measure. Remove a nonempty closed set \(K\) of measure zero, and call the remaining sequences the actual world.

The conjecture says that the actual world can always be divided into blue and gold so that:

- every actual sequence has its color decided by some finite prefix;
- near every missing sequence, blue and gold become equally prevalent.

Precisely, if \([g|n]\) denotes the set of sequences sharing the first \(n\) digits of \(g\in K\), then
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}
\frac{\mu(\text{Blue}\cap[g|n])}{\mu([g|n])}
=\frac12,
\]
uniformly for \(g\in K\).

The distinction would therefore settle everywhere that anything happens, yet become a fair coin at every place where something fails to happen.

The conjecture remains unresolved in the founders’ surviving papers. Their last joint manuscript contains two proposed proofs, both crossed out by both authors.

Beneath them, in different inks:

*Not this way.*

*No. But perhaps near it.*

## Correspondence

### Venn to Rook, 6 February

You keep saying that an unarrival is merely a defect in our choice of \(X\).

Of course one can add the missing thread. One can also repair a torn letter by inserting the words one believes were intended. The result may be consistent. It is not consequently the letter.

The completion remembers no difference between something that happened and something that could always have happened a little longer.

We must remember it for the completion.

Your proof of the converse is correct. I have replaced “phantom” with “unarrival” throughout. “Phantom” grants it too much presence.

### Rook to Venn, 10 February

And “unarrival” grants it a destination.

Nothing in the axioms says the thread was coming.

What we have proved is that finite observations do not exhaust every question we can formulate about them. You speak as though the unanswered remainder were standing outside in the rain.

Still, keep the name. I cannot improve it without making it ugly.

Your alternating-shell construction is lovely. I spent yesterday trying to replace it with something shorter, which is how you may know that I admire it.

### Venn to Rook, 23 February

I do not think it stands outside.

I think “outside” is one of the relations the mathematics invents when it discovers it cannot close the door.

Consider our first example. We see another one, and another, and another. At every stage there is a witness: an actual sequence that agrees this far and then stops. The witnesses need never be the same.

That is the terrible freedom in Axiom III.

We can keep every promise separately and break them all together.

### Rook to Venn, 1 March

The proof is still correct after that sentence, but I distrust what the sentence asks of it.

A sequence that stops did not promise to continue. You have given the observations obligations.

I would rather say: there is no single witness because we asked an infinite question.

But I concede something about the colors. Before your theorem, I thought a missing thread could only be detected by demanding too much. Now we can detect one through a question every actual occurrence answers.

I had not expected absence to make such practical arrangements.

Come on Thursday. I have found the error in our second proof of equal hesitation. It is the same error as in the first proof, wearing your notation.

### Venn to Rook, 4 March

Thursday, then.

We have agreed on every proof for nineteen years, and you still believe the world is innocent of the questions we ask it.

I shall bring the corrected manuscript.

And the blue cup, which you left here. It is an actual object. I have checked at several resolutions.

**Axiom of the remembered departure.**  
Whenever a traveler completes a journey of length \(L>0\) from a location \(a\) to a location \(b\), \(a\) permanently acquires a directed passage to \(b\) of length \(L/2\). Anyone may use this passage. Traveling through a remembered passage is itself a journey.

A journey begins and ends by setting both heels on the ground. This prevents a careless shuffle from making a thousand doors.

The branch of mathematics founded on this axiom is called **vestigial geometry**. Its objects are not spaces alone, but spaces together with what their locations have witnessed. A survey therefore has a date, and usually an hour.

### First consequence: distance need not be mutual

Suppose two previously unvisited locations, \(a\) and \(b\), lie one kilometer apart along an ordinary road.

Someone walks from \(a\) to \(b\).

The road remains one kilometer long. But \(a\) now remembers a departure ending at \(b\), and offers a passage of half a kilometer. Nothing has yet departed from \(b\). Its shortest route back remains the road.

Thus, writing \(d(a,b)\) for the shortest currently available journey,

\[
d(a,b)=\tfrac12\text{ km},
\qquad
d(b,a)=1\text{ km}.
\]

Distance is not a relation between two locations. It is a relation between two locations **in an order**.

This is why milestones have writing on both sides, and why the two sides seldom agree.

### Second consequence: a location can remember a journey no one originally made

Suppose a woman has walked from the well to the orchard, a distance of six hundred meters. Suppose a boy has walked from the orchard to the school, a distance of four hundred meters.

\[
\frac12\left(\frac{600}{2}+\frac{400}{2}\right)=250\text{ meters}.
\]

No one needed to have walked the original thousand-meter route as a single journey. The locations supply the continuity.

\[
\frac14\sum_{i=1}^{n}L_i.
\]

The well does not remember the woman or the boy. It remembers where a departure can end.

=

## The Geometry of Pending Things

The subject began with a remark in the margin of a lighthouse log:

> The supply boat is six miles away. The doctor is six miles away. These are not the same distance.

For several generations, this was treated as an imprecision. Then a keeper named Iona Vey began keeping two columns: **position** and **what is still expected there**.

From these came *expectant geometry*.

Its objects are places equipped with waiting clocks. Its distances depend on the question being asked.

### The three axioms

Let \(d_0(P,Q)\) be the ordinary distance between two places. Choose an expectation \(w\): the arrival of relief, the delivery of a letter, the return of a particular ship.

At each place \(P\), let \(T_w(P)\) be the time when that expectation will be fulfilled. The elementary theory assumes these times are finite, known, and not revised.

At time \(t\), the remaining wait is

\[
r_w(P,t)=\max\{T_w(P)-t,0\}.
\]

**Axiom I — The shore remains.**  
Ordinary distance is a metric. Waiting may add to it, but cannot erase it.

**Axiom II — Clocks run down, not through.**  
An unfulfilled waiting clock loses one hour per hour. Upon fulfillment it stops at zero. Having received a letter yesterday does not put one at minus twenty-four hours of waiting.

**Axiom III — Unequal waiting has length.**  
For a fixed expectation, distance is

\[
\boxed{
d_w(P,Q;t)
=
d_0(P,Q)
+
v\,|r_w(P,t)-r_w(Q,t)|
}
\]

where \(v>0\) converts hours into miles. Each lighthouse district sets its own \(v\), an administrative practice responsible for some very peculiar maps.

This is a genuine metric at every fixed time: the triangle inequality follows from those for ordinary distance and absolute value.

Notice that it is not the *amount* of waiting that separates places. It is the difference. Two keepers each awaiting relief in thirty days are no farther apart, in this geometry, than two keepers whose relief has already arrived.

The early textbooks called this **the cancellation of shared weather**.

---

### One beautiful theorem: The Interval of Unequal Vigil

**Theorem.** The extra distance between two places is exactly \(v\) times the future duration during which one will still be waiting and the other will not.

Suppose fulfillment occurs at times \(a\le b\). Then

\[
\boxed{
d_w(P,Q;t)-d_0(P,Q)
=
v\,\operatorname{length}\bigl([t,\infty)\cap[a,b]\bigr).
}
\]

**Proof.** There are only three cases.

- Before \(a\), the remaining waits are \(a-t\) and \(b-t\). Their difference is \(b-a\).
- Between \(a\) and \(b\), the first clock has stopped. The difference is \(b-t\).
- After \(b\), both clocks read zero.

These are precisely the lengths of the indicated intersection. \(\square\)

The theorem has an initially surprising consequence:

**While both people are waiting, the extra distance does not diminish.**

Both clocks are advancing toward fulfillment, but their difference remains fixed. The distance begins to close only when the first wait ends.

Vey’s proof occupied half a page. Beneath it she wrote:

> The interval belongs to neither arrival.

---

Consider two ships moving east along an ideal, unbounded sea lane, each at one mile per hour.

At time \(t\ge0\), their positions are

\[
x_A(t)=t,
\qquad
x_B(t)=t+4.
\]

Thus their ordinary separation is always four miles. They never meet.

Both crews are waiting to pass the meridian \(x=10\), where they have been instructed to open sealed orders.

Ship \(A\) will pass it at time \(10\). Ship \(B\) will pass it at time \(6\). Take \(v=1\) mile per hour.

Their expectant distance is therefore

\[
d_w(A,B;t)
=
4+
\left|
(10-t)_+-(6-t)_+
\right|,
\]

where \(z_+=\max\{z,0\}\).

Hence

\[
d_w(A,B;t)=
\begin{cases}
8, & 0\le t\le6,\\[2mm]
14-t, & 6\le t\le10,\\[2mm]
4, & t\ge10.
\end{cases}
\]

| Time | Ordinary separation | Wait aboard \(A\) | Wait aboard \(B\) | Expectant distance |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 4 miles | 10 hours | 6 hours | 8 miles |
| 6 | 4 miles | 4 hours | 0 hours | 8 miles |
| 8 | 4 miles | 2 hours | 0 hours | 6 miles |
| 10 | 4 miles | 0 hours | 0 hours | 4 miles |

Between hours six and ten, the ships draw closer without changing their speeds or their separation.

If instead both crews are waiting for the same noon broadcast, their clocks agree, and their expectant distance is four miles throughout.

Thus the question “How far apart are the ships?” is incomplete. One must also ask what they are waiting for.

At hour ten, both sets of orders have been opened. The ships continue east.

---

The feud began when Master Keeper Orrel proposed dispensing with the choice of expectation.

“People wait for many things,” he argued. “Surely their true distance is the smallest distance available under any of them.”

He defined

\[
D(P,Q)=\min_w d_w(P,Q).
\]

He called this **the merciful metric**.

Vey called it “a facility for changing the subject.”

Her counterexample used three lighthouses, \(A,B,C\), situated in that order along a straight coast, one mile apart. Set \(v=1\). Their remaining waits, in hours, were:

| Lighthouse | Until relief arrives | Until next letter arrives |
|---|---:|---:|
| \(A\) | 1 | 11 |
| \(B\) | 1 | 1 |
| \(C\) | 11 | 1 |

For \(A\) and \(B\), choose relief. Their clocks agree:

\[
D(A,B)=1.
\]

For \(B\) and \(C\), choose letters. Their clocks agree:

\[
D(B,C)=1.
\]

But for \(A\) and \(C\), either expectation produces a ten-hour difference:

\[
D(A,C)=2+10=12.

Consequently,

\[
12=D(A,C)>D(A,B)+D(B,C)=2.
\]

The triangle inequality fails.

# Hypnography
*The geometry of places that have always been somewhere else*

Hypnography studies rooms, the distances between them, and the persons required to make those distances exist.

A **room** is a bounded region containing at least one thing you have forgotten. An empty room therefore contains the forgetting itself, usually near the ceiling.

A **door** is not an opening. It is a claim, made by one room, about what comes next.

Distances are measured in *almosts*. One almost is the distance at which you recognize someone before discovering that they are someone else.

## The Three Axioms

**I. The Axiom of Interior Excess**

Every room is strictly larger inside than outside, by exactly the volume of the room in which it is remembered.

If a room is remembered in itself, its volume \(V\) satisfies
\[
V=V+V,\qquad V>0.
\]

Subtraction is permitted, but the two occurrences of \(V\) on the right must not be mistaken for each other. One has a window.

**II. The Axiom of Deferred Adjacency**

Two rooms are adjacent if and only if, upon passing from one to the other, you remember a corridor between them.

The corridor comes into existence behind you. Its length is the time you would have spent traversing it had it existed while you were there.

This length is always exact. Attempts to verify it lengthen the corridor by one childhood afternoon.

**III. The Axiom of Conserved Absence**

In any closed house, the number of people absent is constant.

If a person arrives, someone who was never there becomes absent in their place. This new absence has a name, a preferred chair, and a reason no one mentions it.

An absent person may not be counted twice unless the two counters disagree about whom they are waiting for.

**In every finite house containing one sleeper, there exists a unique room in which the sleeper has already awakened. That room cannot be reached, but every door opens out of it.**

### Proof

Let the sleeper occupy room \(R_0\).

Open a door.

By Deferred Adjacency, this produces both a second room \(R_1\) and a corridor that has now always connected them. Since the corridor did not exist when the sleeper left \(R_0\), the departure cannot yet have happened there. Thus \(R_0\) retains the sleeper’s departure, pending.

Repeat.

Because the house is finite, eventually the sleeper must enter a room already visited. It cannot be the same room: by Interior Excess, each room now contains the memory of a larger house. Therefore what repeats is not the room but the entering.

At this point the house has a closed circuit of entrances and no completed departure.

Someone must be missing.

By Conserved Absence, this cannot be an additional absence. It must be the sleeper’s original absence from the waking world. Transfer that absence to the center of the circuit. Call the resulting room \(W\).

The sleeper is absent from \(W\) in precisely the manner of someone who has just left a bed. Consequently, the sleeper has awakened there.

Now suppose a door led into \(W\). Passing through it would complete one of the pending departures, reducing the number of entrances by one. The circuit would open, releasing the absence on which \(W\) depends. The destination would cease to exist exactly one almost before arrival.

Thus \(W\) cannot be reached.

Nevertheless, any door may be opened while remembering that one has just awakened. Such a door has \(W\) behind it. Hence every door opens out of \(W\).

Uniqueness follows because two awakenings would require a morning between them, and no finite house can contain a morning: mornings have an exterior but no interior.

\[
\boxed{\phantom{\text{The sleeper’s name}}}
\]

The universe is small enough that a misplaced winter can affect everyone.

It has nine inhabited valleys, a salt sea, and a region generally called the north, though compasses indicate it only when carried by visitors. Beneath everything is a dark, porous material that early physicists mistook for stone. It has been stone ever since, to a depth no drill has reached.

Things become more real when they are misunderstood.

This is not the same as believing in them. You can believe in a nonexistent horse all your life without producing so much as a hoofprint. Something has to be there already. You have to encounter it, and get it wrong.

Then it acquires more of the world.

***

For several centuries, reality was measured by weight. This was unsatisfactory. A misunderstood cloud could become more real without getting heavier; instead, it might become impossible to travel beneath without recalling it afterward. Its outline would enter the histories of villages. Rain that had fallen from other clouds would gradually be attributed to it.

Modern instruments measure **insistence**: the degree to which a thing must be taken into account.

A highly real chair need not be large or durable. But a house must be designed around it. People who leave the country continue to arrange their new rooms with a space where it would have stood. Burning it produces ash that cannot be swept under anything.

Understanding diminishes insistence.

Consequently, the sciences are conducted in buildings with very low ceilings and no load-bearing component that anyone has fully described. A good paper on masonry can bring down a laboratory.

There are rigorous conventions for ending an explanation slightly early.

***

A misunderstanding must be sincere.

This was established at considerable expense by the Ministry of Roads, which once employed eleven thousand people to call gravel “bread.” The gravel remained gravel. The workers ate poorly. Several strikes followed.

But a child who thought a milestone was a gravestone gave it such tremendous insistence that the road could no longer pass it. The road curved away over the following week. Its old course is still visible in fields, as a pale strip on which carts become reluctant.

The milestone did not turn into a gravestone. That is another frequent error about this universe. Misunderstanding grants reality, not obedience.

It is still a milestone.

It is simply a milestone that the world cannot afford to leave out.

***

Most domestic inconveniences arise from partial knowledge.

A kitchen drawer sticks because a guest has assumed it contains knives. In fact, it holds string, sealing wax, and the spare mouths for a kettle. By breakfast its contents have gained enough insistence to resist displacement.

A married couple may discover that their bedroom is getting smaller because each has formed a different, inaccurate opinion of the wardrobe. A carpenter can trim it, but that rarely helps for long. Usually they must empty it together and agree on what they find.

Lost objects are troublesome. While searching, people generate sincere hypotheses.

*It must be in the garden.*

*Your brother took it.*

*I think we threw it away.*

A missing needle becomes increasingly difficult to ignore. It pulls at clothing from across a room. At night sleepers turn so that their bodies point toward it. In the worst cases, a house must be abandoned until someone who has never heard of the needle finds it without looking.

For this reason, children are taught to say:

“I don’t know where it is.”

Parents sometimes have to practice saying it too.

***

The most respected profession is that of the **mistaker**.

A mistaker is hired when something necessary has become too well understood.

Bridges are the usual example. A newly built bridge is safe for perhaps thirty years. Engineers inspect it. Travelers become familiar with its sounds. Farmers know exactly which cartloads it will bear. Slowly its insistence declines. It remains intact, but people begin crossing the river without noticing whether they have used it. Water sometimes passes through a pier.

At that stage, a mistaker must be brought in.

The profession requires unusual preparation. Apprentices study maps with errors that their teachers do not correct. They learn several obsolete theories of materials. They are given accurate accounts of distant places, so that their mistaken expectations of the nearby world remain plausible. Each has a different education. A standardized curriculum ruined an entire generation.

The mistaker approaches the bridge alone.

She may conclude that it was built as an aqueduct. She may take the wear of wagon wheels for channels cut by ritual processions. Once, a famous practitioner mistook a bridge for the exposed spine of an animal sleeping beneath the river.

That bridge is still in service.

Mistakers cannot choose their errors, and they cannot be told afterward what they have done. They leave town by a different road. Payment is deposited into an account whose purpose is concealed from them through a long, carefully maintained misunderstanding involving inheritance law.

Their retirement is difficult.

A retired mistaker often has an excellent income, a comfortable house, and no idea why strangers are so grateful to see her.

There are creatures adapted to all this.

The little marsh birds called glasshens are perfectly visible until someone identifies them correctly. Then their insistence falls below that of the reeds, and the eye passes over them. Ornithologists find them by making mistakes about other birds.

Their eggs are protected by resemblance to stones, but only briefly. As soon as the chicks move inside, the resemblance becomes untenable. Parent birds therefore bury the eggs in abandoned nests of other species. A predator that thinks it has found a duck’s egg makes the glasshen chick strong enough to crack its shell.

There is also an animal no one studies anymore.

It lives along the salt shore. It may have legs. Records contradict one another in ways that made it progressively more unavoidable until, for six weeks, every journey in the universe passed through its habitat.

The valleys sent a commission.

The commission returned with a single, plain description, which was read aloud everywhere until ordinary travel resumed.

The description is kept in a locked room. Coastal children learn it before they learn to swim.

***

What the inhabitants find beautiful is a particular kind of absence.

Sometimes an old, very insistent thing is understood all at once.

Not merely identified. Understood in the full shape of its being: what made it, what has happened to it, why it has this crack and not another, what it has prevented, what has leaned against it.

Such understanding almost never occurs. But when it does, the thing relinquishes the world with extraordinary delicacy.

Imagine a great bell vanishing.

You would expect an empty bell tower.

Instead, there is a bell-shaped place where emptiness has less authority. Dust crosses it slowly. A hand put into it feels, not resistance, but permission to stop. Sounds that enter arrive with their edges softened.

The inhabitants call this a **clearance**.

They visit clearances quietly, often with food. Some are public gardens. Others belong to families and are opened only on certain days. A famous clearance in the fourth valley was once a staircase. Visitors climb the steps that remain around it and sit facing the gap.

What they admire is the exactness of the release.

We might notice only that something is missing. They can distinguish a hurried clearance from a patient one. They can see where the understanding faltered and recovered. A flaw near the vanished object’s base may move them more than its perfection elsewhere.

People sometimes spend years trying to understand a thing they love, hoping to grant it this ending.

They are frequently disappointed. Love encourages certain persistent errors.

***

The salt sea contains a clearance so large that it is usually mistaken for weather.

Sailors call it the Pale Reach. It lies west of the central island, though the island itself has become less certain since its lighthouse keeper published his memoirs.

No one knows what the clearance was.

Its outline is visible only in changes of behavior. Ropes laid across a deck within its boundary loosen their knots. People cease interrupting each other. Fish pass through nets without tearing them, and are found later in the hold, apparently having complied with the purpose of fishing rather than its mechanism.

There are no waves in the Reach, but the surface is not flat. Water rises into long, stationary folds. Ships ascend them under sail and descend on the other side. From a distance, their passage looks laborious. Those aboard report no sensation of climbing.

The accepted view is that something enormous was understood there.

The disputed point is what could have understood it.

There were no people when the clearance formed. The oldest coastal deposits already contain salt shaped by its influence.

One theory proposes an animal.

Another proposes that two things, neither alive, came into such exact contact that each fully accounted for the other.

A third is taught only to advanced students, behind screens through which they cannot see their teacher.

***

Last year, a seamstress living above a rope shop bought a small blue bowl.

It was ordinary pottery. The glaze had pooled at the bottom. There was a thumbprint under the rim, and a repair so old that dirt had entered the join.

She used it for pins.

In the evenings, while sewing, she began to notice that she never lost a pin placed inside it. She did not have to count them. She could tip the bowl onto her worktable and feel, with complete confidence, that every pin was there.

After some weeks she recognized the bowl from a dream she had had as a child.

She was wrong about this.

The bowl became harder to move.

She put felt beneath it so it would not scratch the table. Then she moved her sewing to the other end. By autumn the landlord had reinforced the floor, explaining that old houses settle unpredictably near the sea.

One evening she dropped a bent pin beside the bowl.

It fell upward for a short distance, hesitated, and came to rest in the air.

She fetched a chair.

From the chair she could see into the bowl, and beyond its glazed bottom, not through a hole but across a distance that had become available.

There was gray water.

Far away, a ship stood at an angle against the sky. Its sails hung loose. Men on its deck were lowering a long rope over the side.

The seamstress took her hand away from the rim.

The rope continued downward.

She had the strong impression that they were having trouble with its weight. One of the men braced a foot against the rail. Another disappeared below and came back carrying something too small for her to distinguish.

She brought the lamp closer.

On the ship, all the men turned.

There was one unusual law:

**Every separate body of darkness weighed exactly as much as a plum.**

A dark cupboard weighed one plum more than its wood and contents. So did a sealed cavern large enough to contain the town. Divide the cupboard with a lightproof partition, and it gained another plum’s weight. Make a hole in that partition, joining the two darknesses, and the extra weight vanished.

The lacekelp grew hollow black bladders along its stems. Each bladder was much smaller than a pinhead, but contained a full plumweight of darkness. A mature plant could anchor itself against considerable currents without roots.

Small, transparent grazing animals called seamers fed on the bladders’ dividing walls. Their digestion was slow, but the mechanical effect of their feeding was immediate: two neighboring darknesses became one, and the kelp grew lighter.

A heavily grazed stem rose toward the sun.

There it flowered.

Its flowers were transparent except for a dark seam around each seed. When the seed ripened, the seam closed. A new darkness appeared inside it, and the seed dropped sharply to the seabed.

Thus the seamers did not merely eat the kelp. They decided, bladder by bladder, when it was time for the kelp to flower.

Their principal predator was a nearly invisible fish with a luminous mouth. It hunted by putting its head inside a kelp bladder. The light abolished the bladder’s darkness; the stem jerked upward; the seamer lost its grip.

The fish usually missed.

The sea was full of these small, unsuccessful flashes.

***

In town, the commonest domestic inconvenience was the drawer.

A properly closed drawer acquired a plumweight of darkness. Open it, and that weight disappeared. People accustomed to pulling hard on a laden drawer therefore struck themselves in the stomach when it became lighter halfway out.

Fine furniture had tiny windows.

Cheap furniture had bruised owners.

Bakers faced a worse problem. Bread developed enclosed dark pockets as it rose. A modest loaf could become too heavy to lift, although cutting it into slices made it quite manageable.

The town’s staple food was consequently a thin, thoroughly perforated biscuit. There were large loaves on ceremonial occasions, but these were baked on the floor and opened with a saw.

***

A biscuit baker named Venn made the important mathematical discovery.

He wanted a counterweight for his oven door, and had built a lightproof tin box divided into little chambers. Tin was expensive. He wanted the greatest possible weight from the fewest flat partitions.

One partition gave him two darknesses. Two crossing partitions gave him four. Three, carefully placed, gave him eight.

He expected the fourth to give sixteen.

It gave fifteen.

Venn spent two afternoons looking for a light leak. Then he spent eleven years studying divisions of space.

He found that \(n\) flat partitions, arranged as advantageously as possible inside a convex box, could make

\[
1+n+\binom{n}{2}+\binom{n}{3}
\]

separate chambers.

The fourth partition could meet the earlier three along three lines. Those lines could divide it into at most seven regions. It could therefore split seven existing chambers, but not eight.

Venn was delighted by this obstruction. Here was a limit that could not be repaired with better tin.

His little book, *On the Weight of Arrangements*, became popular among builders, who had previously treated partitions as decorative objects with regrettable consequences.

Venn lived above a net-mender named Issa.

Their disagreement concerned the hole in his kitchen floor.

Venn had drilled it to connect the darkness under his floorboards with the darkness above Issa’s ceiling. He maintained that this reduced the strain on the building by one plumweight.

Issa maintained that it let biscuit flour fall into her bed.

Both were correct.

“Put a bend in it,” Venn suggested.

“You put a bend in it.”

“A bend will require a wider opening.”

“Then put the darkness somewhere else.”

Separately, the counterweight and the jar each held one plumweight of darkness.

Connected, they held one between them.

But how much belonged to each?

They put both objects on scales.

At equal heights, each acquired half a plumweight. When Issa lowered her jar, more of the weight settled there. When Venn lifted the counterweight toward the ceiling, it lost nearly all its darkness-weight, though it remained perfectly dark inside.

The darkness was behaving like a liquid with no measurable volume.

They spent the night moving the jar up and down the stairs.

By morning, the oven door had opened and closed forty-three times without anyone touching it. Issa’s best net had been stretched crooked. Neither was speaking to the other, but both had signed the page of measurements.

The discovery explained something about lacekelp that naturalists had long found irritating.

Each plant possessed one immensely long bladder, narrow as a hair, running from its lowest tip to its crown. Earlier investigators had assumed it was a badly formed chamber: so much wall, for only one plumweight.

It was not ballast.

It was a route for ballast.

As a flowering stem bent in a current, the weight of its long darkness moved toward the lower end. If the crown dipped too far, the weight slid toward the crown and pulled it farther down. If the crown remained above the base, the weight stayed at the base and held the plant upright.

The kelp stood poised at a mechanical threshold. One bitten wall could tip it from standing to bowing.

When the sun ripened and dimmed each year, enormous fields of lacekelp bowed together, bringing their flowers down within reach of the seamers. The animals ate the flowers, carried the sticky seeds away, and eventually released them.

For centuries, this had been mistaken for a response to temperature.

She opened it underwater beside a kelp stem and ran black tubes from its chambers into the plant’s bladders. By opening and closing valves, she persuaded a patch of kelp to bow while every other plant remained upright.

The seamers arrived.

So did the luminous fish.

Within an hour, Issa had made a small, misplaced season.

Perhaps there were millions of separate darknesses in the shell.

Perhaps there was only one, connected by passages too narrow to find.

In the deepest accessible fissure, a scientist installed a shutter and a balance. Closing the shutter made the expected difference: one plumweight.

Opening it sometimes removed one plumweight.

Sometimes it removed slightly less.

She checked for damp, friction, air currents, and living things. She replaced the balance. She grew old enough to need help reaching the apparatus.

The discrepancy remained.

Her notebooks ended, year after year, with the same question:

**What lies lower than the bottom of our universe, that some of its darkness should be resting there?**
